content.text:
Tenant database context and filesystem prefixing protect different resources. Stancl’s database bootstrapper changes only Laravel’s default database connection; explicitly selected connections remain untouched. Resetting that context prevents subsequent application work from unintentionally querying the prior tenant’s default database, but it neither changes object-store keys nor removes files.
Filesystem tenancy instead rewrites paths: Stancl suffixes storage_path() and configured disk roots, while Flysystem’s S3 adapter accepts an optional path prefix. This namespaces future filesystem operations under a tenant-specific logical path, but it is not a database guarantee and is not, by itself, an access-control boundary or deletion mechanism.
Queued media conversions prove only that a worker was dispatched or ran under some restored tenant context. Stancl serializes the tenant ID into queued payloads and initializes tenancy when processing; Laravel queues execute jobs asynchronously, may retry/release them, and workers can overlap unless explicitly prevented.
Therefore, deleting a media record or its known files cannot prove physical deletion of outputs written later by an already-running, retried, or duplicated conversion worker. Proving deletion requires cancellation/fencing plus an idempotent generation/version check before write, and a post-quiescence prefix/object inventory sweep with delete permissions. Flysystem’s documented S3 permissions explicitly distinguish PutObject, ListBucket, and DeleteObject; writing capability does not imply cleanup occurred.

Sources:
1. [tenancyforlaravel](https://tenancyforlaravel.com/docs/v3/tenancy-bootstrappers/)
2. [flysystem.thephpleague](https://flysystem.thephpleague.com/docs/adapter/aws-s3-v3/)
